data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The RBNZ pioneered formal inflation targeting in 1990 and mostly kept CPI in its 1-3% band through 2020, with the series low of 0.3% in 2015 and a 2008 peak of 4%. The post-COVID surge broke the pattern: 3.9% in 2021, a series high of 7.2% in 2022 and 5.7% in 2023, driven by housing, supply chains and a tight labour market. The RBNZ was among the first central banks to tighten, lifting the official cash rate from 0.25% to 5.5% between late 2021 and 2023 - a deliberately demand-destroying move that pushed the economy into a shallow recession. It worked: inflation fell to 2.9% in 2024 and a projected 2.8% in 2025, back at the top of the target band. The episode reinforced the RBNZ's hawkish credibility at real output cost.
debt_management: Gross debt rose from 18.4% of GDP in 2006 to 35.7% by 2012, driven by the GFC and the costly Canterbury earthquake rebuild, then fell steadily to 28.1% by 2018 under fiscal consolidation. COVID-era spending pushed it to 43.2% in 2020, and unlike Australia it has kept climbing every year since, reaching a series high of 54.7% in the 2025 projection as post-COVID deficits persisted through weak growth. The level remains low by advanced-economy standards, is NZD-denominated, and has not threatened the sovereign rating; the concern is the trajectory, with deficits now structural rather than cyclical.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis: recession and a sharp rise in debt from 19% to 24.3% of GDP.
February Christchurch earthquake devastated the city and drove a multi-year, debt-funded rebuild.
Jacinda Ardern's Labour-led government took office after the September election, shifting fiscal and housing policy.
March Christchurch mosque attacks - the country's worst mass shooting, prompting rapid gun-law reform.
COVID-19 elimination strategy kept cases near zero but closed borders to tourism and migration.
Aggressive RBNZ tightening to 5.5% tamed 7.2% inflation but pushed the economy into recession.
October election returned a National-led government under Christopher Luxon, pivoting to fiscal restraint.

outlook_next_decade: Inflation is back near target and rate cuts should support a cyclical recovery, but trend growth is held back by weak productivity, housing unaffordability and infrastructure deficits. Debt is likely to stabilize rather than fall quickly unless fiscal consolidation bites. Key uncertainties are dairy and tourism demand from China, migration policy swings, and whether the economy can lift productivity without reigniting house-price inflation. The institutional framework - independent RBNZ, transparent fiscal rules - remains the anchor.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
